1247.title: The Dasam Granth today
1247.hook: it is installed at Takht Hazur Sahib and Takht Patna Sahib, and read by Sikhs
1247.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the Nitnem recite the Jaap Sahib and swayyas in the morning and the Chaupai in the evening, and the Dasam Granth is installed and read at Takht Hazur Sahib and Takht Patna Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Granth and Guru Panth: the Guru's authority placed in the scripture and in the Khalsa gathered before it. Your line was the book and the people.

Before sunrise, in a Sikh home, someone sits with a small prayer book wrapped in cloth. They recite Guru Nanak's Japji, then keep going into words of the Tenth Guru: the Jaap Sahib, a long rush of praise, then a set of swayyas, a different set from the thirty-three met earlier. Some of that morning comes from a book this path has spent weeks in, the Dasam Granth. So where does that book live now, outside the prayer book in someone's lap?
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, A SMALL PRAYER BOOK.` → `INTO THE TENTH GURU'S WORDS.` → `WHERE DOES THE BOOK LIVE NOW?`

segments.voice: Start with two places. One is Nanded, two days back, where Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib stands. The other is Patna, far to the east, where tradition says the Tenth Guru was born, and where Takht Sri Patna Sahib stands. A Takht is a throne, a seat of authority in Sikh life. At both of these Takhts, the Dasam Granth is installed, given a place of honor, and read, alongside the Guru Granth Sahib. So the Tenth Guru's book is honored in a special way at the two places that hold his beginning and his end. Next, the daily prayers. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the shared code of conduct, lists the morning prayers, the Nitnem. Alongside Guru Nanak's Japji, it names compositions from the Dasam Granth: the Jaap Sahib and the swayyas. In the evening prayer there's the Chaupai, a prayer for protection. And at the Amrit ceremony, when Sikhs are initiated into the Khalsa, the Jaap Sahib, the swayyas and the Chaupai are among the prayers recited over the sweetened water, alongside hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib. So the book isn't only on a high seat. It's in mouths and mornings. Third, a careful distinction Sikhs keep. The Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru. The Dasam Granth is honored, read and recited, but it is not the Guru. Holding both, honor without confusing the two, is part of how Sikhs live with this book today. Read and honored: two different things, and both true at once.
screen: `TWO TAKHTS: HIS BIRTH, HIS LAST DAYS.` · `IN THE MORNING AND EVENING PRAYERS.` · `RECITED AT THE AMRIT CEREMONY.` · `HONORED, BUT NOT THE GURU'S SEAT.` · then, large: `READ AND HONORED.`

segments.voice: Picture one Takht, Hazur Sahib on the Godavari, Patna Sahib in the east, or the Akal Takht in Amritsar facing the Golden Temple, and the people walking in this morning, covering their heads and bowing. Rest with that image, and if you pray, join their morning in your own words.
The Dasam Granth today. Installed at Takht Hazur Sahib and Takht Patna Sahib, recited in daily prayers and at the Amrit ceremony, honored alongside the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's word.
Your line: read and honored. Kept on a high seat, and alive in ordinary mornings. Until tomorrow.

1248.title: Holding debates kindly
1248.hook: Sikhs discuss authorship and use of parts of it; the Rehat Maryada guides practice
1248.howItsDone: Sikhs discuss questions about the Dasam Granth in study circles, scholarship and Sikh bodies, while gurdwaras follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada for which compositions are recited in daily prayer and at the Amrit ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dasam Granth today: installed at two Takhts, recited in the daily prayers, honored but not the Guru. Your line was read and honored.

Two cousins at a wedding, plates in hand, have drifted into an argument about a book. One says every page of it is the Guru's own. The other says some parts may come from poets at the court. Voices rise a little. An aunt walks over, hands them both a cup of tea, and says, sit down, and say it again, slowly. That scene, in one form or another, is part of Sikh life with the Dasam Granth. Today isn't about who wins. It's about the tea.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE BOOK.` → `THE GURU'S OWN, OR THE COURT'S?` → `TODAY IS ABOUT THE TEA.`

segments.voice: Here's what Sikhs discuss. First, authorship. Some Sikhs hold that the whole Dasam Granth is the Tenth Guru's own writing. Others hold that some parts may come from the poets around him, and they weigh each composition on its own. Second, use. Which parts belong in public worship, and which are better left for study? Sincere Sikhs, scholars and Sikh bodies have come down in different places, and this lesson takes no side. Now notice what keeps daily life steady while the conversation goes on. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the shared code of conduct, names the compositions that are part of the daily prayers and the Amrit ceremony. That's the maryada at work. The word means a set way, a proper order, the limits that keep things in shape. So a Sikh can join the morning prayers with the sangat without first settling every question about the book. The questions stay open; the practice keeps going. And the Gurus left words about how to talk. Guru Nanak, in a hymn on Ang 661 of the Guru Granth Sahib, says something like this: as long as we're in this world, we should listen to some and say some. Listening first is built right in. Elsewhere Gurbani warns that speaking harshly makes the heart harsh too. Put those together and you get a way of holding a debate. Say what you think. Listen to what they think. Keep the shared practice in the middle, where both of you can stand on it. And bring tea.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one real disagreement you're in, at home, at work or online, and before you rehearse your side, say their view to yourself in their words until it sounds fair. Then find one thing you both stand on, and if you pray, ask in your own words for a gentle tongue.

1249.title: Sword and pen
1249.hook: a warrior who was also a poet, in the same hand
1249.howItsDone: Khalsa Sikhs keep the kirpan as an article of faith alongside daily prayer, and the ideal of the sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier, is taught in gurdwaras and Sikh homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, holding debates kindly: views on the Dasam Granth held side by side, with the shared code keeping practice steady. Your line was disagree kindly.

A hand that has held a bowstring all afternoon picks up a pen at night. The fingers are sore. There's a battle behind and probably another ahead. And the pen moves anyway: praise of the Timeless One, a story of his own life, a ballad, a letter to an emperor. Today, step back from the writings of Guru Gobind Singh and look at the hand itself. The same hand held both.
screen: `A BOWSTRING BY DAY.` → `A PEN BY NIGHT.` → `THE SAME HAND HELD BOTH.`

segments.voice: Sikhs have a name for this pairing: sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier. A sant is a person of devotion. A sipahi is a soldier. The ideal is one person who is both at once, not a soldier on weekdays and a saint on holy days. Think back over the block. The Bachitar Natak tells of battle in verse. The Zafarnama is a letter of rebuke, but it opens with praise of God. And a verse from a composition in the Dasam Granth gathers the two halves into a single plea. Paraphrased, as Sikhs read it, it asks God for a gift: that I never turn away from doing good; that when I go out to face the enemy I have no fear and win; that I teach my own mind to long for Your praise; and that when my time comes, I die fighting in the thick of battle. Listen to the order. Doing good comes first. Courage follows. The mind's longing for praise sits in the middle. Only then the sword. The fighting is for something, and the something is written first. The pairing is still there in Sikh life. A Khalsa Sikh keeps the kirpan, a small sword, as an article of faith, and may carry a prayer book, a gutka, close by too. Neither cancels the other. In this reading, the pen without the sword could be words with no backbone; the sword without the pen, strength with no reason. He kept them in one hand.
screen: `SANT-SIPAHI: THE SAINT-SOLDIER.` · `PRAISE AND BATTLE IN ONE BLOCK.` · `NEVER TURN AWAY FROM DOING GOOD.` · `THE KIRPAN AND THE GUTKA.` · then, large: `PEN AND SWORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you'd stand up for even when it costs you, a person, a principle, a place, and find two or four plain lines about it, no rhyme needed. Write them down or say them over in your head, and notice which line feels strongest.

1250.title: Reading one line of his
1250.hook: pick one line of the Tenth Guru and live with it for a day
1250.howItsDone: Some Sikhs carry the morning hukamnama from the gurdwara as the word for the day, and some take a line from the Nitnem, including the Tenth Guru's compositions, to recall through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sword and pen: the saint-soldier, with doing good written before the sword. Your line was pen and sword.

A tune heard once at breakfast can still be playing in your head at dinner. Nobody learned it on purpose. It was short enough to stay, and by evening it had been everywhere you went. Sikh life has a version of this. In a gurdwara, the morning's hukamnama, one hymn read from the Guru Granth Sahib, is carried home by some Sikhs as the word for the day. Today, try that with the Tenth Guru. Not his whole book. One line.
screen: `A TUNE THAT STAYS ALL DAY.` → `THE WORD FOR THE DAY.` → `NOT THE WHOLE BOOK. ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Here are three lines from his writings, met along the way, each paraphrased. The first is from the Akal Ustat: recognize the whole human race as one. That's a line for a crowded train, for the person you'd rather not sit next to. Live with it for a day and every face becomes a test of it. The second comes from the morning swayyas, which sit in the same work. The Guru says: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. That's a line about the heart under the ritual. Live with it and you start asking where love actually went in what you did. The third is from the Bachitar Natak, about himself. Whoever calls me God, he warns, will fall; I am only the servant of the Supreme. A line about humility, from someone with every reason to be proud. Live with it and watch how often you'd like a little credit. Why only one? Because a line has to be carried to be read. Read a whole page and it stays on the page. Carry one line and it starts reading you back, at the sink, in a meeting, in a mood. That fits a habit in Sikh life: the word isn't finished when the book closes. One line, one day, is enough to find out what the Tenth Guru's words do when they leave the page.

segments.voice: Let the three pass by again, one human race, only those who loved, only the servant, and choose the one that pricks a little, not the one you think is best. Say it slowly in your head, half on the in-breath, half on the out, and if you pray, let it rest beside the name Waheguru.

1251.title: The Tenth Guru's writings close
1251.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Tenth Guru's Jaap Sahib and swayyas in the morning prayers, sing his shabads in kirtan, and hear the Zafarnama and Bachitar Natak in katha, the teaching sessions of the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading one line of his: a single line carried through a whole day until it started reading you back. Your line was one line, one day.

Lay four things on a table. A hymn that won't stop praising. A life story told in verse. A letter that tells an emperor he broke his word. A love song sung in the wilderness. They hardly seem to belong to one person, but they do. For a long run of days this path has been reading Guru Gobind Singh's writings, and today the block closes. Pick up each of the four, then find the thread that runs through them all.
screen: `FOUR THINGS ON A TABLE.` → `ONE PERSON WROTE THEM ALL.` → `ONE THREAD THROUGH THEM.`

segments.voice: Praise first. The Jaap Sahib and the Akal Ustat pour out names for the Timeless One: without mark or sign, without caste or lineage, without color or form. Inside that praise sits the line that recognizes the human race as one. Then autobiography. The Bachitar Natak tells his own story: his father who gave his head but not his faith, the battle at Bhangani, and his warning that no one should call him God, because he is only the servant. Then rebuke. The Zafarnama tells an emperor plainly that oaths were broken, and still holds that no one can harm the one the Lord protects. And song. The ten shabads include the one Sikhs call the song from the wilderness. In paraphrase: tell the beloved Friend how it is with his disciples; without You, fine comforts feel like sickness; a straw bed with the Friend is better than a palace without. Now the thread. All four start from the same place: praise of God, said out loud, without hedging. The letter of rebuke opens with praise. The life story is written in the servant's voice, which is a kind of praise. The love song longs for the Friend. Even in loss, even writing to the man whose armies chased him, the Tenth Guru praises first and boldly. That's one thread a reader can take from this shelf of writings: not a mood of gloom, not a mood of triumph, but praise that doesn't wait for a good day.

1252.title: Who is a Sikh
1252.hook: the Rehat Maryada defines a Sikh as one who believes in One God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib and the Tenth Guru's amrit
1252.tomorrow: The daily banis, in the code
1252.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada opens with a short definition of a Sikh by belief, and Sikh teachers and gurdwara classes often start with it when explaining the code.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tenth Guru's writings closed: praise, story, rebuke and song, all from one pen, all starting with praise. Your line was bold praise.

A hospital intake form has a line that says religion, and a blank about an inch long. One word fits there. But a word in a blank doesn't say what it holds. A family? A country? A list of rules? A feeling? Sikhs have a written answer, at the very start of the shared code met in passing with the rehatnamas: the Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. For the next stretch, the path walks through that code, a piece a day. It begins with a question small enough to fit in the blank. Who is a Sikh?
screen: `ONE WORD IN A BLANK.` → `WHAT DOES THE WORD HOLD?` → `THE CODE BEGINS WITH A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here is the code's answer, in paraphrase. A Sikh is any human being who faithfully believes in one Immortal Being; in the ten Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh; in the Guru Granth Sahib; in the words and teachings of the ten Gurus; and in the amrit, the initiation the Tenth Guru gave; and who holds to no other religion as their own. Start with the first words: any human being. The door isn't marked with a caste, a birthplace, a family name or a language. None of those appear in the list at all. Then look at what is there. One God. The teachers. The book where the teaching now lives. The teaching itself. And the Tenth Guru's initiation. Now the verb: believes. On the amrit, the definition asks for belief in the initiation the Tenth Guru gave. Some readers point out that this leaves room for a person who holds that path as true and has not yet walked through it; the code speaks about those who have taken amrit, and what is asked of them, in its own later sections. Then the word itself. Tradition says a sikh is a learner, a disciple. Read that way, the definition is a learner's list, running in a line from God to the person reading. And notice how short it is. A child could learn it. A grown person could hold it up against their own life and see where they stand. The code could have opened with rules. It opens with belief, plainly put, and the rules come after.

1253.title: The daily banis, in the code
1253.hook: the code lists the morning, evening and night banis
1253.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep nitnem recite the morning banis after waking, Rehras in the evening and Sohila before sleep, often from a gutka or from memory; some communities add further banis to the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who is a Sikh: any human being who holds the code's beliefs, plainly put, with the rules after. Your line was belief, plainly put.

On an old sailing ship, a bell was struck at set times through the day and night, so everyone aboard knew where the day stood without looking for a clock. The day had marks in it, and the marks held the crew together. The code gives the Sikh day its marks too: which prayers are said, and when. Morning, evening, night.
screen: `A BELL AT SET HOURS.` → `THE DAY HAS MARKS IN IT.` → `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The daily set is called nitnem, the daily rule. Each piece in it is a bani, a composition of the Gurus. In paraphrase, here's the code's list. In the morning: Japji Sahib, the Jaap Sahib, and the Ten Swayyas, the ones that begin with the words sravag sudh. In the evening: Sodar Rehras, a gathering of hymns read as the day goes down. At night, before sleep: Sohila. Part of this list came up a few days ago, from the Tenth Guru's side. Now look at all of it, and at who is speaking. Japji Sahib is Guru Nanak's, the first words of the Guru Granth Sahib. The Jaap Sahib and the Swayyas are the Tenth Guru's, the writings of the last few weeks. So the morning opens with the first Guru and the Tenth side by side, the beginning of the line and its end, before breakfast. Then the shape. Three doors in the day: one as it starts, one as it turns toward dark, one as it closes. Nobody has to decide each day whether to pray or what to say. The code has already set the table. One caution. The code's list is a shared floor, not a ceiling. Some Sikh communities and schools add more banis to the morning, and families keep their own additions. The code names what Sikhs agree on together. So the stretch that began with the Tenth Guru's own writings ends with two of them set into a daily timetable. They aren't only studied. They're said aloud, morning after morning.
